title: From Atlanta to Montgomery: A New Generation Rides for Voting Rights
summary: The echoes of 1965 were unmistakable. On Saturday, May 16, 2026, two buses rolled from Atlanta to Montgomery, Alabama, carrying dozens of activists determined to revive the fight for voting rights. Their journey mirrored the final leg of the historic Selma-to-Montgomery march, where civil rights protesters were brutally beaten before eventually securing the Voting Rights Act. This time, the catalyst was a 6-3 Supreme Court ruling that declared considering race in redistricting is itself discriminatory. The decision struck down a majority-Black congressional district in Louisiana, and several states—including Alabama—quickly redrew maps that dilute Black voting power. For Keith Odom, 62, who traveled from South Carolina, the trip was personal. "I'm not trying to live a life that's going backwards," he said. "I want to go forward, for my grandchildren." The rally, dubbed "All Roads Lead to the South," was organized by Fair Fight Action, the group founded by Stacey Abrams. It drew a cross-section of generations: Justice Washington, a college student named for her family's faith in the justice system; Kobe Chernushin, an 18-year-old white organizer filming for social media; and Darrin Owens, 27, a political operative who attended as a citizen. "Political activism is personal," Owens said. "I'm committed to action that stops what I consider un-American." The buses departed from Georgia's 5th district, once represented by John Lewis, who was beaten on Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge at age 25. A proposed federal bill bearing his name could override the Supreme Court and reinvigorate voting protections, but its fate is uncertain. As riders arrived in Montgomery, there were no federal troops—unlike in 1965. The fight, they know, is now in their hands.
why_it_matters: Voting rights determine who has a voice in government; when courts change the rules on redistricting, it can affect which communities gain or lose political power — decisions that will shape the world young people inherit.

keywords.explanation: A catalyst is something that causes a major event or change to happen.
Discriminatory means unfairly treating a group of people differently, often based on race or background.
Redistricting is the process of drawing new boundaries for voting districts, which can affect who gets elected.
To dilute means to make something weaker or less powerful, like adding water to juice or reducing a group's voting strength.
An operative is someone who works behind the scenes in politics to influence plans and strategies.
To reinvigorate means to give new energy or strength to something that has become weaker.

background_read: On March 7, 1965, civil rights marchers crossing Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge were violently attacked by state troopers, an event now called "Bloody Sunday."
The outrage led to the Selma-to-Montgomery marches, which pressured Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — a law that banned racial discrimination in voting.
In 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 4(b) of the Voting Rights Act in Shelby County v. Holder, saying its coverage formula was outdated; critics say this weakened voting protections.
The 2026 Supreme Court ruling mentioned in the article further limited the use of race in redrawing congressional districts, arguing that considering race is itself a form of discrimination.
John Lewis (1940–2020) was not only a civil rights leader beaten on Bloody Sunday but also served as a U.S. congressman for Georgia's 5th district for over 30 years.

perspectives.description: The march brought together a new generation of activists across races and ages, showing that the fight for equality remains alive and can be energized. Organizers like Fair Fight Action see the rally as a powerful way to draw attention to voting rights at a critical moment.

The Supreme Court's ruling has made it easier to dismantle districts that historically allowed minority communities to elect candidates of their choice. Critics warn this could reverse decades of progress and silence Black voters in several states.

The tension between state-level redistricting and federal voting protections is a long-standing feature of American democracy. The pendulum has swung back and forth since the 1960s, reflecting shifting judicial philosophies about race and representation.

The fate of the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act could redefine the landscape. If passed, it could restore federal oversight; if not, activists may need to focus on state-level organizing and litigation to protect voting access.
